trial_name: PReVENT — Low vs Intermediate Tidal Volume in ICU Patients Without ARDS (2018)
citation: Simonis FD, Serpa Neto A, Binnekade JM, Braber A, Bruin KCM, Determann RM, et al; Writing Group for the PReVENT Investigators. Effect of a low vs intermediate tidal volume strategy on ventilator-free days in intensive care unit patients without ARDS: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018;320(18):1872-1880
one_liner: In ICU patients without ARDS, a low tidal volume strategy (4–6 mL/kg) did not improve ventilator-free days or mortality compared with an intermediate, pressure-limited strategy (8–10 mL/kg), and significantly increased hypercapnic harm.

pico.population: Adults receiving invasive ventilation without ARDS, expected to require ventilation >24 hours
pico.intervention: Low tidal volume strategy targeting 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight
pico.comparison: Intermediate tidal volume strategy targeting 8–10 mL/kg predicted body weight (with pressure limit)

background.existing_knowledge: Low tidal volume ventilation improves outcomes in ARDS, and ventilator-induced lung injury is biologically plausible even in non-ARDS lungs. Observational studies and meta-analyses suggested low tidal volumes might benefit non-ARDS patients, but evidence was heterogeneous and confounded.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a low tidal volume strategy improves patient-centred outcomes in ICU patients without ARDS compared with a pressure-limited, intermediate tidal volume strategy.
background.hypothesis: Low tidal volume strategy would increase ventilator-free days at day 28 compared with an intermediate strategy.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, multicentre, parallel-group, open-label, randomised controlled trial in 6 ICUs in the Netherlands.
methods.setting: 6 ICUs in the Netherlands; randomisation required within 1 hour of start of invasive ventilation in the ICU.

exclusion: Invasive ventilation >12 hours before ICU admission
History of pulmonary disease (severe COPD, pulmonary fibrosis)

methods.intervention: Low tidal volume strategy targeting 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight. Volume-controlled ventilation started at 6 mL/kg, decreased by 1 mL/kg per hour to minimum 4 mL/kg. Pressure support: lowest support achieving target (minimum 5 cm H2O); tidal volume >8 mL/kg accepted if minimal support. Adjustments permitted for dyspnoea; additional sedation or muscle relaxants not allowed.
methods.comparison: Intermediate tidal volume strategy targeting 8–10 mL/kg predicted body weight (initially 10 mL/kg). If plateau pressure exceeded 25 cm H2O, tidal volume reduced to maintain plateau ≤25 cm H2O. Pressure support adjusted to target tidal volume with max airway pressure <25 cm H2O. Other ventilator settings (PEEP, FiO2) and weaning per local practice with protocolised daily assessment.
methods.blinding: Open-label; ventilator settings not concealable. Outcomes collected without blinding, but weaning/extubation criteria were protocolised.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 952 patients (476/group) to detect a 1-day difference in ventilator-free days (SD 5) with 80% power at 5% significance, allowing 20% dropout. 961 were randomised.
secondary_outcomes: Duration of ventilation among survivors to day 28
ICU length of stay among survivors
Hospital length of stay among survivors
Rescue therapy for hypercapnia or severe respiratory acidosis
methods.follow_up: Through day 90 for mortality; ICU and hospital discharge for length of stay.

headline_bullets: Primary outcome neutral: identical mean ventilator-free days at day 28 (21.0 vs 21.0; mean difference −0.27, 95% CI −1.74 to 1.19; P=0.71).
Low tidal volume group had significantly more severe respiratory acidosis (17.8% vs 10.3%; RR 1.54; P=0.001) and more rescue therapy for hypercapnia/acidosis.
No significant difference in mortality at day 28 (12.8% vs 11.5%; HR 1.12; P=0.30) or day 90 (19.6% vs 17.1%; HR 1.08; P=0.45).
Pre-specified subgroup: among patients intubated in ICU, low tidal volume associated with fewer ventilator-free days (mean difference −2.50, 95% CI −4.63 to −0.36; interaction P=0.01).

outcomes_table.outcome: Duration of ventilation among survivors to day 28, median (IQR) [days]
ICU length of stay among survivors, median (IQR) [days]
Hospital length of stay among survivors, median (IQR) [days]
Rescue therapy for severe respiratory acidosis

safety: Low tidal volume group experienced significantly more severe respiratory acidosis (pH <7.25): 17.8% vs 10.3%, RR 1.54 (95% CI 1.20–1.98, P=0.001).
Rescue therapy for hypercapnia was more frequent in low tidal volume arm (1.9% vs 0.2%, RR 7.70, P=0.02).
Rescue therapy for severe respiratory acidosis also more frequent (4.8% vs 1.5%, RR 2.89, P=0.02).
No significant difference in ARDS, pneumonia, or delirium (delirium: 43.4% vs 36.6%, RR 1.15, P=0.06).

domains.notes: Web-based randomisation with variable block sizes (2–6), stratified by centre and location of intubation. Allocation concealment adequate.

Open-label; ventilator settings visible. Primary endpoint (ventilator-free days) influenced by clinician decisions. Weaning/extubation criteria were protocolised, and mortality outcomes objective, reducing but not eliminating risk.
961 randomised, primary outcome data available for 955 (475 vs 480). Attrition minimal (2 vs 4 lost); ITT analysis used.
Clear separation in tidal volume early, narrowing by day 3 as patients transitioned to assisted modes. Additional sedation/muscle relaxants to achieve protocol not permitted.
Groups comparable: SAPS II median 52 vs 51, PaO2/FiO2 197 vs 198, baseline tidal volume 7.0 vs 7.3 mL/kg PBW. Most intubated outside ICU (72.1% vs 70.3%).

domains.domain: Separation of the variable of interest
domains.notes: Achieved: median delivered tidal volume after titration 5.9 (5.2–6.7) vs 9.1 (7.9–10.0) mL/kg PBW; day 1, day 2, day 3 showed separation, P<0.001 for overall. Driving pressure also lower (12 vs 13 cm H2O, mean difference −1.23, P<0.001).
Power calculation met; no interim analyses; multiple secondary endpoints without adjustment. Subgroup analysis pre-specified but vulnerable to multiplicity.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong: robust randomisation, minimal attrition, clear early separation; main threats are open-label design for a process-mediated endpoint and narrowing separation over time in a short-ventilation-duration population.

domains.notes: Conducted in 6 Dutch ICUs; predominantly older adults with mixed indications (high proportion coma/cardiac arrest). Excluded patients with chronic pulmonary disease, prolonged pre-ICU ventilation >12 h, uncontrolled intracranial hypertension – limits applicability to these groups.

Most applicable to high-resource ICUs with frequent ventilator reassessment and early transition to assisted modes. Comparator was pressure-limited, not traditional high tidal volumes (12 mL/kg). May not apply to settings where usual care involves higher tidal volumes without pressure limits.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate: findings generalise well to similar adult ICU populations without ARDS in comparable systems, but applicability is limited in patients with chronic lung disease, prolonged pre-ICU ventilation, or where usual care differs substantially from the intermediate pressure-limited comparator.

strengths: Large, pragmatic multicentre RCT in a common ICU population.
Early enrolment (median <1 hour from initiation of ventilation) enhances causal attribution.
Clear early physiologic separation (tidal volume, plateau pressure, driving pressure) between groups.
Clinically relevant primary endpoint (ventilator-free days) with near-complete follow-up.
Protocolised weaning/extubation criteria to minimise performance bias.
limitations: Open-label intervention with a process-dependent primary endpoint susceptible to bias.
Comparator was an intermediate, pressure-limited strategy, not traditional high tidal volumes; contrast may be insufficient.
Treatment separation narrowed by day 3 (median 7.3 vs 9.1 mL/kg PBW), potentially diluting sustained low-tidal-volume effect.
Many eligible patients not enrolled for logistical reasons, introducing selection effects.
Secondary outcomes and subgroup analyses not adjusted for multiplicity; borderline signals require caution.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted pragmatic trial showing no benefit of low tidal volume ventilation over an intermediate, pressure-limited strategy in patients without ARDS, with evidence of harm from hypercapnic acidosis. Methodological strengths include early randomisation and minimal attrition; main limitation is open-label design and limited sustained separation.
strengths: Clear early tidal volume separation achieved
Protocolised weaning to limit performance bias
weaknesses: Open-label design for a process-dependent primary endpoint

sections.authors_conclusion: For ICU patients without ARDS, targeting very low tidal volumes (4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight) did not improve ventilator-free days or mortality versus an intermediate, pressure-limited approach, but increased severe respiratory acidosis and use of rescue therapies.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routinely targeting very low tidal volumes (4–6 mL/kg PBW) in non-ARDS ICU patients adds harm (hypercapnia, acidosis) without improving ventilator-free days or mortality compared with a pressure-limited strategy targeting 8–10 mL/kg PBW. This trial supports avoiding aggressive tidal volume reduction if it causes respiratory acidosis.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU patients without ARDS receiving invasive ventilation, particularly those with relatively short expected ventilation duration and without chronic lung disease.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Low tidal volumes are harmful in ARDS or that any reduction below 8 mL/kg is always harmful; rather, routine ultra-low targets (<6 mL/kg) in non-ARDS patients may cause unnecessary hypercapnic harm when the comparator is already pressure-limited.
implementation_caveats: If targeting lower tidal volumes, monitor for respiratory acidosis and be prepared to adjust to avoid pH <7.25.
The trial excluded patients with pre-existing pulmonary disease and those ventilated >12 hours before ICU admission; generalisability limited in those groups.
The comparator was pressure-limited, not traditional high tidal volumes; in settings where usual care is higher, the risk–benefit may differ.

controversies.topic: Pre-trial meta-analyses suggested benefit of lower tidal volumes in non-ARDS, challenged by neutral PReVENT result
controversies.notes: Observational data and meta-analyses had supported low tidal volumes for non-ARDS. PReVENT’s neutral findings contradict that, highlighting the limitations of non-randomised evidence and the importance of empirical RCTs.

controversies.topic: Tension between physiological separation (lower driving pressures) and clinical outcomes
controversies.notes: Despite significant reductions in plateau and driving pressures, no improvement in patient-centred outcomes was observed, raising questions about surrogate endpoints and the translation of physiological benefit to clinical benefit.

controversies.topic: Comparison with RELAx trial on PEEP strategies in non-ARDS
controversies.notes: RELAx similarly found no improvement in ventilator-free days with lower vs higher PEEP in non-ARDS patients, reinforcing that extrapolating ‘more protective’ ventilator settings to non-ARDS populations requires empirical confirmation and may introduce harms.

controversies.topic: Guidelines continue to recommend lung-protective tidal volumes (≤8 mL/kg) but caution against ultra-low volumes (4–6 mL/kg) due to PReVENT
controversies.notes: Contemporary international guidance often recommends tidal volumes ≤8 mL/kg PBW as default for all ventilated patients, but PReVENT supports avoiding routine escalation to very low tidal volumes in non-ARDS patients when they produce hypercapnic harm without clear benefit.

context_related_trials.relation: A related RCT in ICU patients without ARDS comparing lower vs higher PEEP strategies. Also found no improvement in ventilator-free days, reinforcing that more protective ventilator settings do not necessarily improve outcomes in this population and that competing harms must be considered.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal tidal volume target in patients with moderate hypoxemia but not meeting ARDS criteria?
Is there a benefit of driving pressure-guided ventilation in non-ARDS?
Would sustained low tidal volumes show benefit in patients with longer ventilation duration or higher baseline risk of lung injury?
What is the impact of early versus late initiation of low tidal volume?
Are there subgroups (e.g., sepsis, trauma) where low tidal volume may be beneficial despite overall neutral results?

numbers_to_remember: Ventilator-free days identical: 21.0 vs 21.0 (mean diff −0.27, 95% CI −1.74 to 1.19)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In ICU patients without ARDS, low tidal volume (4–6 mL/kg PBW) ventilation does not improve outcomes and causes more hypercapnic harm compared with a pressure-limited intermediate strategy (8–10 mL/kg PBW).
